title: CUET Computer Science Test 3
subject: Computer Science / Informatics Practices
syllabus_source: CUET SYLLABUS/Computer Science - 308.pdf (NTA syllabus for CUET (UG) 2026, latest published)
past_paper_reference: Pattern benchmark only: CUET (UG) 2025 308 paper structure and formats (no questions copied)
instructions: Attempt all 15 questions of Section A.
Then attempt all 35 questions of EITHER Section B1 (Computer Science) OR Section B2 (Informatics Practices) — 50 questions in total.
Each correct answer earns 5 marks; each incorrect answer deducts 1 mark; unattempted questions earn 0.

sections.title: Section A — Database Concepts, SQL and Computer Networks (compulsory)

questions.question:
What is the output of the following MySQL query?

SELECT RIGHT('COMPUTER', LENGTH('ABC'));
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) TER
Given: The inner function is evaluated first.
Step 1: LENGTH('ABC') = 3
Step 2: RIGHT('COMPUTER', 3) = the last 3 characters = 'TER'
Common mistake: (A) uses LEFT(). (B) takes 4 characters. (D) stops after LENGTH().
Key point: LEFT(str, n) and RIGHT(str, n) take n characters from either end.

questions.question: Table RESULT has 6 rows. The Marks column has the values 35, 72, 18, 90, 39 and 40. After running DELETE FROM RESULT WHERE Marks < 40;, how many rows remain?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3
Given: DELETE removes only the rows that satisfy the WHERE condition.
Step 1: Marks < 40 → 35, 18, 39 → 3 rows deleted
Step 2: Remaining: 72, 90, 40 → 3 rows (40 is not less than 40)
Common mistake: (A) ignores the DELETE. (B) assumes all rows go, as without WHERE. (C) also deletes 40.
Key point: DELETE is a DML command; the table structure remains.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): A table can have more than one primary key.
Reason (R): A table can have more than one candidate key.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
Why: The Assertion is false — although a relation may have several candidate keys (the Reason is true), only ONE of them is chosen as the primary key; the remaining candidate keys are called alternate keys.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) need a true Assertion.
Key point: A primary key may be composite (made of more than one attribute) but there is still only one primary key.

questions.question:
Arrange the following milestones in the evolution of networking in chronological order:
(A) ARPANET connects computers of universities and research centres
(B) NSFNET is created for academic research
(C) The World Wide Web is invented by Tim Berners-Lee
(D) TCP/IP becomes the standard protocol of ARPANET
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (D), (B), (C)
Why: NCERT's timeline: ARPANET began in 1969 (A); TCP/IP was adopted as its standard protocol in 1982–83 (D); NSFNET was created in 1986 (B); and the WWW was invented in 1990 (C).
Why not the others: (B) puts NSFNET before TCP/IP. (C) puts TCP/IP before ARPANET. (D) puts the WWW before NSFNET.
Key point: The Internet grew as many such networks were interconnected.

questions.question: Which of the following is a database management system (DBMS)?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) MySQL
Why: NCERT gives MySQL, Oracle, PostgreSQL, SQL Server and MongoDB as examples of DBMS software, used to create and manage databases.
Why not the others: (A) is a word processor. (B) is a web browser. (D) is an editor for writing Python programs.
Key point: MySQL is an open-source relational DBMS.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Term)
(A) Relation
(B) Tuple
(C) Attribute
(D) Domain

List-II (Meaning)
(I) A column of a table
(II) The set of all allowed values for an attribute
(III) A table with rows and columns
(IV) A row of a table
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(II)
Why: In the relational model, a relation is a table (III); a tuple is a row (IV); an attribute is a column (I); and a domain is the set of values an attribute can take (II), e.g. the domain of Gender may be {M, F, T}.
Why not the others: (A) swaps tuple and attribute; (C) swaps relation and tuple; (D) swaps attribute and domain.
Key point: The number of attributes is the degree; the number of tuples is the cardinality.

questions.question:
Table STUDENT:

Name | Class | Marks
Ira | 12 | 78
Om | 11 | 85
Jay | 12 | 91
Kia | 11 | 67

What is the FIRST row of the output of SELECT Name FROM STUDENT ORDER BY Class, Marks DESC; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Om
Given: Rows are sorted on Class (ascending, the default) first; rows with the same Class are sorted on Marks descending.
Step 1: Class 11 comes before Class 12 → Om (85), Kia (67)
Step 2: Within Class 11, higher marks first → Om, then Kia
Step 3: First row → Om
Common mistake: (A) sorts only on Marks DESC. (B) sorts Marks ascending within the class. (C) starts with Class 12.
Key point: DESC applies only to the column it follows.

questions.question: In SQL, the result of SELECT City FROM CLUB1 MINUS SELECT City FROM CLUB2; (written EXCEPT in some systems) is:
options: A) Cities that appear in both CLUB1 and CLUB2
B) Cities that appear in CLUB1 but not in CLUB2
C) All cities of CLUB1 and CLUB2 without duplicates
D) Every pairing of a city of CLUB1 with a city of CLUB2
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Cities that appear in CLUB1 but not in CLUB2
Why: NCERT explains that the MINUS (set difference) operation returns the rows produced by the first query that are not produced by the second.
Why not the others: (A) is INTERSECT. (C) is UNION. (D) is a Cartesian product.
Key point: MINUS is not commutative: CLUB1 − CLUB2 ≠ CLUB2 − CLUB1 in general.

questions.question: A network that connects computers spread across a city, such as a cable TV network, is a:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) MAN
Why: NCERT classifies networks by the area covered: PAN (a few metres, around one person), LAN (a room, building or campus), MAN (a city, up to about 30–40 km) and WAN (across countries).
Why not the others: (A) covers a few metres. (C) covers a building or campus. (D) covers a very large area such as a country.
Key point: The Internet is the largest WAN.

options: A) New tables that the query creates and saves in the database
B) Names of the two columns shown in the result of the query
C) Short temporary names (aliases) for STUDENT and CLASS
D) Constraints that check the join condition on each row
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Short temporary names (aliases) for STUDENT and CLASS
Why: An alias is a temporary name given to a table (or column) within a query. Here S stands for STUDENT and C for CLASS, which makes the query shorter and makes clear which table each column belongs to.
Why not the others: (A) No tables are created. (B) The result columns are Name and Teacher. (D) Aliases are not constraints.
Key point: A column alias uses AS, e.g. SELECT Sal * 12 AS Annual.

questions.question: A family wants to connect its computer to the Internet through a telephone line, which carries analog signals. Which device converts the computer's digital signals into analog form and back?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Modem
Why: NCERT explains that a modem (MOdulator–DEModulator) converts digital data from the computer into analog signals for transmission (modulation) and converts received analog signals back into digital data (demodulation).
Why not the others: (A) and (C) connect devices within a LAN. (B) regenerates weak signals.
Key point: Modulation is digital → analog; demodulation is analog → digital.

questions.question: Relation R has tuples with the values {a, b, c, d, e} and relation S has {b, d, f} (both have the same single attribute). What are the cardinalities of R ∩ S and R − S?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 2 and 3
Given: R ∩ S keeps tuples present in both; R − S keeps tuples of R that are not in S.
Step 1: R ∩ S = {b, d} → cardinality 2
Step 2: R − S = {a, c, e} → cardinality 3
Common mistake: (B) swaps the two. (C) gives R ∪ S (6) for the first. (D) computes S − R for the second.
Key point: Set operations need union-compatible relations.

questions.sub_topic: Nested text functions — LOWER and MID
questions.question:
What is the output of the following MySQL query?

SELECT LOWER(MID('INFORMATICS PRACTICES', 13, 9));
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) practices
Given: 'INFORMATICS' has 11 characters, position 12 is the space, so 'PRACTICES' starts at position 13.
Step 1: MID(…, 13, 9) = 'PRACTICES'
Step 2: LOWER('PRACTICES') = 'practices'
Common mistake: (A) takes the first word. (C) skips LOWER(). (D) starts two positions too early.
Key point: LCASE() is the same as LOWER().

questions.question:
Table STUDENT has a column Class with the values XI, XII, XI, X, XII, XI. How many rows are returned by:

SELECT Class, COUNT(*) FROM STUDENT GROUP BY Class;
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3
Given: GROUP BY makes one output row for each distinct value of the grouping column.
Step 1: Distinct classes: X, XI, XII
Step 2: Rows returned = 3 (counts 1, 3 and 2)
Common mistake: (B) counts the table rows. (C) treats it like COUNT(*) without GROUP BY. (D) misses one class.
Key point: Every non-aggregate column in SELECT should appear in GROUP BY.

questions.sub_topic: Effect of constraints in CREATE TABLE
questions.question:
A table is created with:

CREATE TABLE STUDENT (RollNo INT PRIMARY KEY, Name VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL, Fee FLOAT DEFAULT 1000, Email VARCHAR(30) UNIQUE);

Consider the following statements:
(A) A row inserted without a value for Fee will get Fee = 1000.
(B) Two students can have the same Email.
(C) Name cannot be left NULL.
(D) Two students can have the same RollNo.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A) and (C) only
Why: DEFAULT supplies 1000 when Fee is not given (A); NOT NULL forbids a missing Name (C).
Why not the others: Statement (B) is false — UNIQUE does not allow duplicate e-mails. Statement (D) is false — a PRIMARY KEY must be unique and not NULL. Options (B), (C) and (D) include one or both.
Key point: PRIMARY KEY = UNIQUE + NOT NULL.

questions.question: Many antivirus programs detect known malware by:
options: A) Increasing the speed of the Internet connection
B) Deleting all files that have not been opened recently
C) Comparing files with a database of known malware signatures
D) Encrypting every file on the computer
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Comparing files with a database of known malware signatures
Why: NCERT explains that antivirus software identifies malware mainly by signature-based detection — matching code against a database of known malware patterns — and also by watching for suspicious behaviour (heuristics). The database must be updated regularly.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (D) are not how antivirus software works.
Key point: An out-of-date antivirus cannot detect new malware by signature.

questions.question:
Table EMP has a row with Name = 'Ravi' and Sal = 25000. What does the following query show for Ravi?

SELECT Name, Sal * 12 AS Annual FROM EMP WHERE Name = 'Ravi';
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Ravi, 300000
Given: Arithmetic can be done in SELECT; AS gives the computed column a heading.
Step 1: Sal * 12 = 25000 × 12 = 300000
Step 2: The column heading is Annual; the value shown is 300000
Common mistake: (A) ignores the multiplication. (B) adds 12. (D) prints the heading as the value.
Key point: The stored Sal value does not change.

questions.sub_topic: Number of swaps in bubble sort
questions.question: How many swaps does bubble sort make to sort [4, 3, 2, 1] in ascending order?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 6
Given: Bubble sort swaps adjacent elements that are out of order.
Step 1: Pass 1: (4,3), (4,2), (4,1) → 3 swaps → [3, 2, 1, 4]
Step 2: Pass 2: (3,2), (3,1) → 2 swaps → [2, 1, 3, 4]
Step 3: Pass 3: (2,1) → 1 swap → [1, 2, 3, 4]; total = 3 + 2 + 1 = 6
Common mistake: (A) counts only the first pass. (B) counts elements. (D) has no basis.
Key point: A list in reverse order is the worst case for bubble sort: n(n − 1)/2 swaps.

questions.question: The daily sales (in units) for five days are 12, 15, 9, 20 and 14. What is the mean?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 14
Given: Mean = sum of values ÷ number of values.
Step 1: Sum = 12 + 15 + 9 + 20 + 14 = 70
Step 2: Mean = 70 ÷ 5 = 14
Common mistake: (A) is the middle value as listed. (C) is the range. (D) is the sum.
Key point: The mean uses every value, so it is affected by extreme values.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question: A TV remote control sends signals to the TV over a short distance and needs a clear line of sight. Which type of transmission does it use?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Infrared
Why: NCERT notes that infrared waves are used for very short-distance communication, such as TV remotes, and need line of sight; they cannot pass through walls.
Why not the others: (B) and (C) are wired media. (D) is used for long-distance communication.
Key point: Bluetooth uses radio waves for short-range communication without line of sight.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Operation)
(A) PUSH
(B) POP
(C) ENQUEUE
(D) DEQUEUE

List-II (Action)
(I) Remove an element from the front of a queue
(II) Add an element at the rear of a queue
(III) Add an element at the top of a stack
(IV) Remove an element from the top of a stack
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: PUSH adds at the top of a stack (III) and POP removes from the top (IV); ENQUEUE adds at the rear of a queue (II) and DEQUEUE removes from the front (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps PUSH and POP; (B) swaps ENQUEUE and DEQUEUE; (C) swaps POP and ENQUEUE.
Key point: Stack — one end; queue — two ends.

questions.sub_topic: Insertion sort on a sorted list
questions.question:
Assertion (A): Insertion sort makes only n − 1 comparisons when the list is already sorted in ascending order.
Reason (R): For a sorted list, each element is compared only with the element just before it and no shifting is needed.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: When the list is sorted, every new element is already larger than the last element of the sorted part, so one comparison per pass is enough and nothing is shifted. With n − 1 passes, there are n − 1 comparisons. The Reason explains the Assertion.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both are true.
Key point: This makes insertion sort good for nearly sorted data.

questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

q = []
for i in range(1, 5):
    q.append(i * i)
q.pop(0)
q.pop(0)
print(q[0], q[-1])
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 9 16
Given: range(1, 5) gives 1, 2, 3, 4; pop(0) dequeues from the front.
Step 1: q = [1, 4, 9, 16]
Step 2: Two pop(0) calls remove 1 and 4 → q = [9, 16]
Step 3: Front q[0] = 9; rear q[-1] = 16
Common mistake: (B) and (C) ignore the dequeues. (D) dequeues from the rear.
Key point: In a list-based queue, q[0] is the front and q[-1] is the rear.

questions.question: Before deleting an element from a queue, the dequeue() function should first check:
options: A) Whether the queue is full
B) Whether the queue is empty
C) Whether the queue is sorted
D) Whether the front element is the largest
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Whether the queue is empty
Why: Deleting from an empty queue is an underflow situation, so dequeue() should first check isEmpty() and report an error or return None if there is nothing to remove.
Why not the others: (A) matters only for insertion into a fixed-size queue. (C) and (D) are not needed for a queue.
Key point: A Python list-based queue never becomes 'full', but it can become empty.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(A) Snooping
(B) Eavesdropping
(C) Ethical (white-hat) hacker
(D) Cracker (black-hat hacker)

List-II
(I) Breaks into systems illegally with malicious intent
(II) Finds security weaknesses with the owner's permission so that they can be fixed
(III) Listening to or intercepting a private conversation or message in real time without permission
(IV) Secretly capturing and analysing network traffic
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: NCERT describes snooping as the secret capture and analysis of network traffic (IV); eavesdropping as unauthorised real-time interception of private communication such as a call or message (III); an ethical hacker as one who finds weaknesses legally to improve security (II); and a cracker as one who breaks in with bad intentions (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps snooping and eavesdropping; (C) swaps eavesdropping and ethical hacker; (D) swaps ethical hacker and cracker.
Key point: Encryption protects data against snooping and eavesdropping.

questions.question: A stack is used to check whether the brackets in ((a+b)*(c-d)) are balanced: '(' is pushed, and each ')' pops one '('. What is the largest number of elements on the stack at any time?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2
Given: Only the brackets matter.
Step 1: '(' '(' → stack size 2; ')' → 1
Step 2: '(' → 2; ')' → 1; ')' → 0
Step 3: The maximum size reached is 2, and the stack is empty at the end, so the expression is balanced
Common mistake: (B) counts all opening brackets as if none were popped. (A) and (C) miscount the nesting.
Key point: The brackets are balanced if the stack is empty at the end and no pop was attempted on an empty stack.

questions.sub_topic: Identifying a sorting algorithm from code
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Selection sort
Why: In each pass, the code finds the position m of the smallest element in the unsorted part L[i:] and swaps it into position i. This is selection sort.
Why not the others: (B) swaps adjacent elements repeatedly. (C) shifts elements to insert one value. (D) is a searching technique.
Key point: Selection sort makes at most n − 1 swaps.

questions.sub_topic: Output of a linear search function
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 1 -1
Given: The function returns the index of the FIRST match, or −1 if no element matches.
Step 1: For k = 8, L[1] = 8 is the first match → returns 1
Step 2: For k = 5, no element matches → the loop ends and −1 is returned
Common mistake: (A) and (D) return the last match. (C) returns 0 for 'not found'. (D) also forgets the final return.
Key point: Returning inside the loop stops the search at the first match.

questions.question:
Arrange the following stages of handling data in the correct order:
(A) Store the data in a file or database
(B) Collect the data, e.g. through a survey
(C) Process the data to get useful information
(D) Present the results, e.g. as a table or chart
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (A), (C), (D)
Why: NCERT describes data being collected (B), stored (A), and processed to obtain information (C), which is then presented or interpreted for decision-making (D).
Why not the others: (A) stores before collecting. (B) processes before storing. (D) presents before processing.
Key point: Processing turns raw data into information.

questions.question: Which of the following is the best real-life example of LIFO (Last-In-First-Out)?
options: A) People standing in a line at a bus stop
B) Vehicles passing through a toll gate one by one
C) Students entering a hall in order of roll numbers
D) A pile of plates, where the plate placed last is taken first
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) A pile of plates, where the plate placed last is taken first
Why: NCERT uses a pile of plates or books as an example of a stack: new items are placed on top, and the top item is removed first.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) are first-come-first-served, i.e. FIFO (queues).
Key point: Insertion and deletion in a stack happen at the same end, the TOP.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question: Two buildings of a company are 1.5 km apart. The link must carry data at very high speed and must not be affected by electrical interference from heavy machines. Which medium is most suitable?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Optical fibre cable
Why: Optical fibre carries data as light, so it supports very high bandwidth over long distances and is immune to electromagnetic interference.
Why not the others: (A) is affected by interference and is meant for short distances. (B) and (C) are very short range.
Key point: Optical fibre is costly and needs care during installation.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II for a student sending an e-mail to a teacher:

List-I (Component)
(A) Sender
(B) Message
(C) Communication medium
(D) Protocol

List-II (Example)
(I) The Wi-Fi and cables that carry the data
(II) The student's computer
(III) The set of rules, such as SMTP, followed to send the e-mail
(IV) The text and attachment of the e-mail
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(II), (B)-(IV), (C)-(I), (D)-(III)
Why: NCERT lists the components of data communication: sender (the device sending data, II), receiver, message (the data sent, IV), communication medium (the path, I) and protocol (the rules, III).
Why not the others: (A) swaps sender and message; (B) swaps medium and protocol; (D) swaps message and medium.
Key point: The teacher's computer is the receiver.

questions.topic: B1: Computer Networks and Data Communication
questions.question:
Assertion (A): The bandwidth of a communication channel is measured in Hertz (Hz).
Reason (R): The data transfer rate is measured in bits per second (bps).
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: Both statements are true. NCERT defines bandwidth as the range of frequencies available for transmission on a channel, so it is measured in Hz, kHz, MHz and so on. The data transfer rate (bps, Kbps, Mbps) is a different quantity; the Reason states a separate fact and does not explain why bandwidth is measured in Hertz.
Why not the others: (A) The Reason does not explain the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both statements are true.
Key point: Higher bandwidth generally allows a higher data transfer rate.

questions.sub_topic: Choosing a primary key from a scenario
questions.question: A hospital table PATIENT has the columns Name, Age, City and AadhaarNo. Which column is the most suitable primary key?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) AadhaarNo of the patient
Why: A primary key must be unique and not NULL for every row. Each person has a different Aadhaar number, whereas names, ages and cities can repeat among patients.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) can have the same value for two patients.
Key point: Choose an attribute that will never repeat and is always known.

questions.question: Binary search is applied to a sorted list of 64 elements. If the key is not found in the first three comparisons, at most how many elements are left to be searched?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 8
Given: Each unsuccessful comparison discards about half of the remaining elements.
Step 1: After comparison 1 → about 32 elements remain
Step 2: After comparison 2 → about 16
Step 3: After comparison 3 → about 8
Common mistake: (A) and (B) stop after one or two halvings. (D) removes only one element per comparison, as in linear search.
Key point: This halving is why binary search needs only about log₂ n comparisons.

questions.question: Table CUSTOMER has a column City with the values Pune, Agra, Pune, Delhi, Agra, Pune. How many rows are returned by SELECT DISTINCT City FROM CUSTOMER; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 3
Given: DISTINCT removes duplicate values from the result.
Step 1: Distinct cities: Pune, Agra, Delhi
Step 2: Rows returned = 3
Common mistake: (B) counts all rows. (C) misses one city. (D) assumes only one row.
Key point: DISTINCT does not change the stored data.

questions.question: What is the value of the prefix expression − * 3 4 + 2 1 ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 9
Given: In prefix notation, each operator comes before its two operands.
Step 1: * 3 4 = 12
Step 2: + 2 1 = 3
Step 3: − 12 3 = 9
Common mistake: (A) evaluates 12 − 2 + 1. (B) adds instead of subtracting. (C) multiplies 3 by (4 + 2 + 1).
Key point: A prefix expression can be evaluated with a stack by scanning from right to left.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) NULL is the same as an empty string ''.
(B) A condition such as Phone = NULL does not find rows where Phone is NULL.
(C) IS NULL is used to test whether a value is NULL.
(D) Aggregate functions other than COUNT(*) ignore NULL values.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: NULL means a missing or unknown value. Comparing anything with NULL using = gives an unknown result, so Phone = NULL finds nothing (B); IS NULL / IS NOT NULL must be used (C); and SUM, AVG, MAX, MIN and COUNT(column) skip NULLs (D).
Why not the others: Statement (A) is false — '' is a known value (an empty string), whereas NULL means no value. Options (A), (B) and (D) include it.
Key point: NULL is not 0 and not ''.

questions.sub_topic: DDL and DML commands by purpose
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Command)
(A) ALTER
(B) UPDATE
(C) DROP
(D) DELETE

List-II (Purpose)
(I) Removes rows from a table
(II) Changes the values stored in existing rows
(III) Changes the structure of a table
(IV) Removes a table along with its structure
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: ALTER changes structure, e.g. adds a column (III); UPDATE changes data values (II); DROP removes the whole table (IV); DELETE removes rows (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps ALTER and UPDATE; (C) swaps DROP and DELETE; (D) swaps UPDATE and DROP.
Key point: ALTER and DROP are DDL; UPDATE and DELETE are DML.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about staying safe online:
(A) Using the same password for all accounts is a safe practice.
(B) The operating system and antivirus software should be kept updated.
(C) Important data should be backed up regularly.
(D) A firewall helps block unauthorised network access.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: NCERT lists safety measures such as updating software to fix known weaknesses (B), regular backups so data can be recovered after an attack such as ransomware (C), and using a firewall (D).
Why not the others: Statement (A) is false — if one account is compromised, the same password exposes all the others. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Use strong, different passwords and change them periodically.

questions.question:
Relation STUDENT:

RollNo | Name | Marks
1 | Arun | 85
2 | Bina | 72
3 | Charu | 91
4 | Dev | 80

What is the result of π Name (σ Marks > 80 (STUDENT)) ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Arun, Charu
Given: The inner operation is done first.
Step 1: σ Marks > 80 selects the tuples with Marks 85 (Arun) and 91 (Charu); 80 is not greater than 80
Step 2: π Name keeps only the Name attribute → Arun, Charu
Common mistake: (A) ignores the selection. (C) includes 80. (D) projects RollNo instead of Name.
Key point: σ chooses rows, then π chooses columns.

questions.sub_topic: Searching with hashing — order of steps
questions.question:
Arrange the steps to search for a key in a hash table:
(A) Compute the hash value h(key)
(B) Go to the slot of the table given by the hash value
(C) Compare the element stored in that slot with the key
(D) Report 'found' if they match, otherwise 'not found'
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B), (C), (D)
Why: The hash function is applied to the key first (A); its value gives the slot to look in directly (B); the element there is compared with the key (C); and the result is reported (D). No other positions need to be scanned when there is no collision.
Why not the others: (B) goes to a slot before computing it. (C) compares before reaching the slot. (D) compares before hashing.
Key point: The same hash function is used to store and to search.

questions.sub_topic: Best and worst cases of searching
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) In the best case, binary search finds the key with just one comparison.
(B) In the best case, linear search needs n comparisons for a list of n elements.
(C) In the worst case, binary search needs about log₂ n comparisons.
(D) Binary search cannot be applied directly to an unsorted list.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A), (C) and (D) only
Why: Binary search's best case is the key at the middle — 1 comparison (A); its worst case is about log₂ n comparisons because the list is halved each time (C); and it needs a sorted list (D).
Why not the others: Statement (B) is false — linear search's BEST case is the key at the first position, 1 comparison; n comparisons is its worst case. Options (A), (B) and (C) include it.
Key point: Linear search: best 1, worst n. Binary search: best 1, worst about log₂ n.

Answer: (B) len(st) == 0
Why: Underflow happens when we try to pop from an empty stack. len(st) == 0 is True exactly when the stack is empty, so the message is printed instead of popping.
Why not the others: (A) prints 'Underflow' when the stack is NOT empty. (C) pops an element while testing. (D) An empty list is not None.
Key point: An isEmpty() function usually returns len(st) == 0.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) Mean, median and mode are measures of central tendency.
(B) Range and standard deviation are measures of variability (spread).
(C) Two data sets with the same mean must have the same standard deviation.
(D) If the standard deviation of a data set is 0, all its values are equal.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: NCERT groups mean, median and mode as measures of central tendency (A) and range and standard deviation as measures of variability (B). A standard deviation of 0 means no value differs from the mean, so all values are equal (D).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — e.g. {5, 5, 5} and {1, 5, 9} both have mean 5 but different spreads. Options (B), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: A measure of spread tells how far values lie from the centre.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) T 2.0 F
Given: int("5") = 5, which is not negative; 10 / 5 raises no exception.
Step 1: try prints T; r = 10 / 5 = 2.0 (the / operator always gives a float)
Step 2: No exception → else prints 2.0
Step 3: finally prints F → T 2.0 F
Common mistake: (A) uses integer division. (B) assumes an exception. (D) forgets that finally runs.
Key point: The else block runs only when the try block raises no exception.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) T V F
Given: int("abc") cannot convert the text to a number.
Step 1: try prints T, then int("abc") raises ValueError
Step 2: The except ValueError block prints V
Step 3: finally prints F → T V F
Common mistake: (B) uses the wrong handler. (C) assumes the error is not handled. (D) forgets that T was printed before the error.
Key point: Statements in try before the error still run.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) T Z F
Given: int("0") = 0, which is not negative.
Step 1: try prints T; 10 / 0 raises ZeroDivisionError
Step 2: Python checks the except clauses in order: ValueError does not match; ZeroDivisionError matches → prints Z
Step 3: else is skipped; finally prints F → T Z F
Common mistake: (A) uses the first except clause regardless of type. (B) assumes 10 / 0 = 0. (C) assumes no handler matched.
Key point: Only the first matching except clause runs.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) T V F
Given: int("-2") = −2, so the condition n < 0 is True.
Step 1: try prints T; the raise statement raises ValueError("negative")
Step 2: The except ValueError block catches it and prints V
Step 3: finally prints F → T V F
Common mistake: (A) assumes division by zero. (C) ignores the raise statement and divides. (D) assumes a raised exception cannot be caught.
Key point: The raise statement throws an exception deliberately; it is handled like any other exception.

questions.topic: B1: Exception and File Handling in Python
options: A) T V F is printed, and the program continues
B) T Z F is printed, and the program continues
C) T F is printed, and then the program stops with a TypeError
D) Nothing is printed, because the error occurs before try
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) T F is printed, and then the program stops with a TypeError
Given: TypeError matches neither except clause.
Step 1: try prints T; int(None) raises TypeError
Step 2: No handler matches, so else is skipped, but finally still runs and prints F
Step 3: The exception is then passed on (propagated) to the caller; as nobody handles it, the program stops with a TypeError traceback
Common mistake: (A) and (B) assume some handler catches it. (D) The error occurs inside try, after T is printed.
Key point: finally runs even when an exception is not handled.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Library or software)
(A) NumPy
(B) Pandas
(C) Matplotlib
(D) MySQL

List-II (Mainly used for)
(I) Storing data in a relational database and querying it with SQL
(II) Plotting graphs and charts
(III) Fast numerical computation on arrays
(IV) Data analysis with Series and DataFrames
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(IV), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: NCERT describes NumPy as the library for numerical arrays (III), Pandas for data analysis using Series and DataFrames (IV), and Matplotlib for visualisation (II); MySQL is a relational DBMS used with SQL (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps NumPy and Pandas; (B) swaps Pandas and Matplotlib; (D) swaps Matplotlib and MySQL.
Key point: Pandas is built on top of NumPy.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.sub_topic: max() and min() of a column
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
t = pd.DataFrame({'Temp': [31, 28, 35, 30]})
print(t['Temp'].max() - t['Temp'].min())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 7
Given: max() and min() give the largest and smallest values of the column.
Step 1: max = 35; min = 28
Step 2: 35 − 28 = 7 (the range)
Common mistake: (B) is the maximum alone. (C) subtracts the first two values. (D) is the first value.
Key point: The range shows how spread out the data are.

questions.question: Which of the following is a web browser?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Mozilla Firefox
Why: NCERT lists Google Chrome, Mozilla Firefox, Safari and Microsoft Edge as web browsers — software used to access and view websites.
Why not the others: (A) is a DBMS. (B) is a spreadsheet program. (C) is a programming language.
Key point: Browser settings let users manage cookies, history and the default search engine.

questions.question: Table MEMBER has a column JoinDate with the values '2021-06-15', '2023-01-09', '2022-11-30'. What is the output of SELECT MAX(JoinDate) FROM MEMBER; ?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2023-01-09
Given: For dates, MAX() gives the latest date and MIN() the earliest.
Step 1: In order: 2021-06-15, 2022-11-30, 2023-01-09
Step 2: Latest = 2023-01-09
Common mistake: (A) is MIN(). (C) compares only the month and day. (D) is COUNT().
Key point: The 'YYYY-MM-DD' format sorts dates correctly.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.sub_topic: Reading and writing MySQL tables from Pandas
questions.question:
Consider the following statements about Pandas and MySQL:
(A) read_sql() can only read an entire table; it cannot run an SQL query.
(B) to_sql() writes the data of a DataFrame into a MySQL table.
(C) A connection to the database must be created before read_sql() or to_sql() is used.
(D) With if_exists='append', to_sql() adds the rows to an existing table.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (B), (C) and (D) only
Why: NCERT shows to_sql() writing a DataFrame into a table (B), using a connection created first with a connector such as pymysql or sqlalchemy (C); if_exists='append' adds rows, while 'replace' recreates the table (D).
Why not the others: Statement (A) is false — read_sql() can run any SELECT query, e.g. pd.read_sql('SELECT * FROM student WHERE Marks > 80', con). Options (A), (B) and (C) include it.
Key point: Data can move both ways between MySQL and Pandas.

questions.question: A school's computers suddenly show a message: "Your files are locked. Pay ₹50,000 to get the key." Which cybercrime is this?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Ransomware attack
Why: NCERT describes ransomware as malware that encrypts or blocks access to a victim's data and demands a ransom payment to restore access.
Why not the others: (B) is copying someone's work. (C) is posting provocative comments. (D) is unauthorised use of a copyrighted work.
Key point: Regular backups reduce the damage of ransomware.

questions.question:
What is the output of the following MySQL query?

SELECT YEAR('2023-11-05') + MONTH('2023-11-05');
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) 2034
Given: YEAR() returns 2023 and MONTH() returns 11, both as numbers.
Step 1: YEAR('2023-11-05') = 2023
Step 2: MONTH('2023-11-05') = 11
Step 3: 2023 + 11 = 2034
Common mistake: (A) adds the day (5). (B) joins the digits as text. (D) skips MONTH().
Key point: DAY() would return 5.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
s = pd.Series([10, 20, 30])
print(s.index.tolist())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) [0, 1, 2]
Given: When no index is given, Pandas uses the default integer index starting from 0.
Step 1: Three values → index 0, 1, 2
Common mistake: (B) starts from 1. (C) lists the values. (D) mixes index and values.
Key point: A custom index can be given with index=[…].

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.sub_topic: mode() with more than one mode
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
print(pd.Series([3, 1, 3, 2, 1]).mode().tolist())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) [1, 3]
Given: mode() returns ALL the values with the highest frequency, in sorted order.
Step 1: Frequencies — 3: twice; 1: twice; 2: once
Step 2: Both 1 and 3 occur most often → [1, 3]
Common mistake: (A) and (B) return only one of the two modes. (D) is the median.
Key point: mode() returns a Series, even when there is one mode.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question: In for i, row in df.iterrows():, what are i and row in each iteration?
options: A) The column label and the column as a Series
B) The row position and the column names
C) The row index label and the row's data as a Series
D) The first and the last value of each row
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) The row index label and the row's data as a Series
Why: NCERT explains that iterrows() goes through a DataFrame row by row, giving each row's index label together with the row's data as a Series.
Why not the others: (A) describes iterating over columns with items() (iteritems() in older versions). (B) and (D) do not describe iterrows().
Key point: Inside the loop, row['Maths'] gives that row's Maths value.

questions.question:
Table NUM has a column N with the values 3, 8, 12, 7 and 10. What is the output of:

SELECT COUNT(*) FROM NUM WHERE MOD(N, 2) = 0;
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 3
Given: MOD(N, 2) = 0 is true for even numbers.
Step 1: Even values: 8, 12, 10
Step 2: COUNT(*) = 3
Common mistake: (A) counts the odd values. (B) counts all rows. (C) assumes no row matches.
Key point: Functions can be used inside WHERE conditions.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
df = pd.DataFrame({'A': [1, 2], 'B': [3, 4]})
df['C'] = df['A'] + df['B']
print(df['C'].tolist())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) [4, 6]
Given: Assigning to a new column label adds that column; arithmetic on columns is done row by row.
Step 1: Row 0: 1 + 3 = 4
Step 2: Row 1: 2 + 4 = 6
Common mistake: (A) adds down the columns. (C) lists all values. (D) adds everything.
Key point: df.drop('C', axis=1) would remove the new column.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Function)
(A) NOW()
(B) ROUND()
(C) TRIM()
(D) COUNT()

List-II (Category)
(I) Aggregate function
(II) Math (numeric) function
(III) Date function
(IV) Text (string) function
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(IV), (D)-(I)
Why: NCERT groups single-row functions into math (ROUND, POWER, MOD — II), text (UPPER, TRIM, MID — IV) and date (NOW, DAY, MONTHNAME — III) functions; COUNT, like SUM and AVG, is an aggregate function (I).
Why not the others: (A) swaps NOW and ROUND; (C) swaps ROUND and TRIM; (D) swaps TRIM and COUNT.
Key point: Single-row functions return one value per row; aggregates return one value per group.

questions.sub_topic: Safe practice on a shared computer
questions.question: Which is a safe practice when using a computer in a cyber café?
options: A) Saving passwords in the browser so that logging in is quicker next time
B) Logging out of all accounts and clearing the browsing history before leaving
C) Leaving the e-mail account open so that it loads faster the next time
D) Writing the password on a small note and sticking it on the monitor
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) Logging out of all accounts and clearing the browsing history before leaving
Why: NCERT advises that on public or shared computers, one should not save passwords, should log out of all accounts, and should clear the browsing history so that the next user cannot access one's accounts.
Why not the others: (A), (C) and (D) let the next user misuse the accounts.
Key point: Prefer browsing in private (incognito) mode on public computers.

questions.question: A frequency polygon is drawn by:
options: A) Plotting separate points for pairs of values of two variables
B) Dividing a circle into slices, one for each class interval
C) Joining the mid-points of the tops of histogram bars with lines
D) Drawing a box from the first quartile to the third quartile
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Joining the mid-points of the tops of histogram bars with lines
Why: NCERT explains that a frequency polygon is a type of line graph obtained by joining the mid-points of the tops of the adjacent bars of a histogram. It shows the shape of a frequency distribution.
Why not the others: (A) is a scatter plot. (B) is a pie chart. (D) is a box plot.
Key point: Frequency polygons make it easy to compare two distributions on one graph.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) A Series is a one-dimensional labelled data structure.
(B) A DataFrame is a two-dimensional labelled data structure.
(C) The size of a Series can be changed, but its values cannot.
(D) Both the size and the values of a DataFrame can be changed.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: NCERT describes a Series as 1-D (A) and a DataFrame as 2-D (B). In a DataFrame, values can be changed and rows or columns can be added or removed, so both size and values are mutable (D).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — it is the other way round: a Series' VALUES are mutable but its SIZE is immutable. Options (A), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Each column of a DataFrame is a Series.

questions.question:
Assertion (A): HTML is used to design the structure of web pages.
Reason (R): HTML is a programming language used for server-side database processing.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
Why: The Assertion is true — HTML (HyperText Markup Language) uses tags to describe the structure and content of a web page. The Reason is false — HTML is a markup language, not a programming language, and it does not process databases on the server; languages such as PHP or JSP are used for that.
Why not the others: (A) and (B) need a true Reason. (D) The Assertion is true.
Key point: Static web pages are written in HTML; dynamic pages also use scripting languages.

questions.sub_topic: GROUP BY with ORDER BY on an aggregate
questions.question:
Table EMP:

Name | Dept | Sal
A | HR | 300
B | IT | 500
C | HR | 400
D | Sales | 650
E | IT | 300

What is the FIRST row of the output of:

SELECT Dept, SUM(Sal) FROM EMP GROUP BY Dept ORDER BY SUM(Sal) DESC;
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) IT, 800
Given: Each department's salaries are added, and then the groups are sorted by the total, highest first.
Step 1: HR = 300 + 400 = 700; IT = 500 + 300 = 800; Sales = 650
Step 2: In descending order of total: IT 800, HR 700, Sales 650
Step 3: First row → IT, 800
Common mistake: (B) sorts on the single highest salary. (C) is the second row. (D) shows only one HR salary.
Key point: ORDER BY can use an aggregate function.

questions.question: A caller claiming to be from a bank asks a customer to share the OTP received on the phone to 'update KYC'. What should the customer do?
options: A) Share the OTP, since the caller knows the account number
B) Share only the first three digits of the OTP
C) Send the OTP by SMS instead of telling it on the call
D) Refuse to share it, because banks never ask for OTPs, and report the call
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) Refuse to share it, because banks never ask for OTPs, and report the call
Why: NCERT warns that OTPs, passwords and PINs must never be shared. Fraudsters often pretend to be bank staff (a form of phishing called vishing) to get OTPs and steal money.
Why not the others: (A), (B) and (C) all give the fraudster access to the OTP.
Key point: Report such frauds to the bank and the cybercrime helpline.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I (Network)
(A) PAN
(B) LAN
(C) MAN
(D) WAN

List-II (Example)
(I) The Internet connecting countries
(II) A cable TV network across a city
(III) The computers of a school's computer lab
(IV) A phone connected to wireless earphones over Bluetooth
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A)-(IV), (B)-(III), (C)-(II), (D)-(I)
Why: A PAN covers a few metres around one person (IV); a LAN covers a room or building (III); a MAN covers a city (II); and a WAN covers countries — the Internet is the largest WAN (I).
Why not the others: (B) swaps PAN and LAN; (C) swaps LAN and MAN; (D) swaps MAN and WAN.
Key point: Networks are classified by the area they cover.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.sub_topic: Steps of a simple data analysis
questions.question:
Arrange the following steps of analysing sales data stored in sales.csv:
(A) Plot the totals as a bar chart
(B) Remove rows with missing values using dropna()
(C) Read the file using pd.read_csv('sales.csv')
(D) Find the total sales of each region using groupby()
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (C), (B), (D), (A)
Why: The data must first be loaded (C), then cleaned (B), then summarised (D), and finally the summary is visualised (A).
Why not the others: (A) groups before cleaning, so incomplete rows affect the totals. (B) cleans before the data are read. (D) plots before computing the totals.
Key point: Cleaning data before analysis gives reliable results.

questions.question:
Match List-I with List-II:

List-I
(A) Plagiarism
(B) Copyright infringement
(C) Trademark infringement
(D) Public domain work

List-II (Example)
(I) Selling shoes that carry a famous brand's logo without permission
(II) Using a film song in a video without the owner's permission
(III) Submitting an essay copied from a website as one's own
(IV) A work whose copyright has expired, which anyone can use freely
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) (A)-(III), (B)-(II), (C)-(I), (D)-(IV)
Why: Presenting copied work as one's own is plagiarism (III); using a copyrighted song without permission is copyright infringement (II); misusing a brand's mark is trademark infringement (I); and works whose copyright has ended are in the public domain (IV).
Why not the others: (A) swaps plagiarism and copyright infringement; (B) swaps copyright and trademark infringement; (D) swaps trademark infringement and public domain.
Key point: Always give credit to the source when using others' work.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements:
(A) An e-mail address has the form username@domain, e.g. asha@example.com.
(B) An e-mail can be sent to only one recipient at a time.
(C) An e-mail can be delivered only if the receiver is online at that moment.
(D) Chat allows people to exchange text messages in real time.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (A) and (D) only
Why: NCERT describes the e-mail address format (A) and chat as real-time text communication over the Internet (D).
Why not the others: Statement (B) is false — an e-mail can be sent to many recipients using To, Cc and Bcc. Statement (C) is false — e-mail is stored on the mail server and read whenever the receiver logs in. Options (A), (B) and (C) include one or both.
Key point: E-mail is asynchronous; chat is synchronous (real time).

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
Assertion (A): For a DataFrame df with a column 'Maths', df['Maths'] returns a Series.
Reason (R): Each column of a DataFrame is a Series, sharing the DataFrame's row index.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
options: A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
B) Both Assertion and Reason are true, but Reason is not the correct explanation of Assertion
C) Assertion is true, but Reason is false
D) Assertion is false, but Reason is true
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) Both Assertion and Reason are true, and Reason is the correct explanation of Assertion
Why: A DataFrame can be thought of as a collection of Series objects, one for each column, all sharing the same index. Selecting one column with df['Maths'] therefore returns that Series. The Reason explains the Assertion.
Why not the others: (B) The Reason explains the Assertion. (C) and (D) Both are true.
Key point: df[['Maths']] (a list of labels) returns a DataFrame instead.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
print(pd.Series([10, 20, 30, 40, 50]).quantile(0.25))
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) 20.0
Given: quantile(0.25) gives the first quartile (Q1), the value below which 25% of the sorted data lie; Pandas uses linear interpolation.
Step 1: Position = 0.25 × (5 − 1) = 1 → the element at index 1 of the sorted data
Step 2: Q1 = 20.0
Common mistake: (B) averages 20 and 30. (C) is the median (Q2). (D) is 25% of 50.
Key point: quantile(0.75) gives Q3, which is 40.0 here.

questions.question:
Arrange the following stages of a school project in the correct order:
(A) Develop the solution
(B) Identify the problem
(C) Present the results
(D) Plan the work and divide tasks among team members
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) (B), (D), (A), (C)
Why: NCERT's approach to a project begins with identifying the problem (B), then planning and dividing the work (D), then developing and testing the solution (A), and finally presenting the results (C).
Why not the others: (A) develops before planning. (C) plans before knowing the problem. (D) presents before the solution is built.
Key point: Teamwork and regular communication help at every stage.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question: A CSV file data.csv has no header line — its first line already holds data. Which statement reads it correctly?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) pd.read_csv('data.csv', header=None)
Why: By default, read_csv() treats the first line as column names (header=0). With header=None, the first line is read as data and the columns are labelled 0, 1, 2 … (names can be supplied using names=[…]).
Why not the others: (A) index=False is a to_csv() option. (B) would use the first data line as column names. (C) writes a file; it does not read one.
Key point: sep=';' can be given when the values are separated by semicolons.

questions.question:
Consider the following statements about technology and health:
(A) Looking at a screen for long periods without breaks can cause eye strain.
(B) Sitting with poor posture for long hours can cause back and neck pain.
(C) Keeping the monitor very close to the eyes reduces eye strain.
(D) Spending excessive time online can lead to Internet addiction.
Choose the correct answer from the options given below:
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) (A), (B) and (D) only
Why: NCERT discusses eye strain from long screen use (A), body pain from poor posture (B) — reduced by ergonomically designed furniture — and Internet addiction (D).
Why not the others: Statement (C) is false — the monitor should be at a comfortable distance; very close viewing increases eye strain. Options (B), (C) and (D) include it.
Key point: Take regular breaks and maintain a correct posture.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – I
questions.question:
d1 has 2 rows and the columns x and y; d2 has 3 rows and the same columns. What is printed by:

c = pd.concat([d1, d2])
print(c.shape, c.index.tolist())
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) (5, 2) [0, 1, 0, 1, 2]
Given: concat() places the rows of d2 below those of d1 and keeps each original index unless ignore_index=True.
Step 1: Rows = 2 + 3 = 5; columns stay x and y → shape (5, 2)
Step 2: Index = d1's [0, 1] followed by d2's [0, 1, 2]
Common mistake: (A) places the frames side by side in the shape. (B) keeps only one frame. (C) assumes the index is renumbered.
Key point: pd.concat([d1, d2], ignore_index=True) gives the index 0 to 4.

questions.topic: B2: Data Handling using Pandas – II
questions.question:
What is printed by the following code?

import pandas as pd
p = pd.DataFrame({'Region': ['N', 'S', 'N', 'S', 'N'],
                  'Year': [2023, 2023, 2024, 2024, 2024],
                  'Sales': [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]})
pt = p.pivot_table(index='Region', columns='Year', values='Sales', aggfunc='sum')
print(pt.loc['N', 2024])
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 80
Given: pivot_table() puts Region on the rows and Year on the columns, and adds the Sales of matching rows (aggfunc='sum').
Step 1: Rows with Region N and Year 2024: Sales 30 and 50
Step 2: Sum = 80
Common mistake: (A) and (D) take only one of the two rows. (C) adds all N rows, including 2023.
Key point: pivot() would raise an error here because (N, 2024) occurs twice; pivot_table() aggregates duplicates.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A shop owner draws a chart of yearly sales (in ₹ lakh) of two branches:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
year = [2020, 2021, 2022, 2023]
north = [40, 55, 50, 70]
south = [30, 35, 60, 65]
plt.plot(year, north, color='green', linestyle='dashed', marker='o', label='North')
plt.plot(year, south, color='red', linewidth=3, label='South')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Sales')
plt.title('Branch Sales')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Question: How many lines are drawn on the chart?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2
Given: Each plt.plot() call draws one line on the same figure.
Step 1: plt.plot(year, north, …) → one line
Step 2: plt.plot(year, south, …) → second line
Common mistake: (A) counts the years. (B) assumes the second plot replaces the first. (C) counts the data points.
Key point: All plot() calls before show() appear on the same figure.

Question: In which year were South's sales higher than North's?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (B) 2022
Given: Compare the two lists year by year.
Step 1: 2020: 30 < 40; 2021: 35 < 55
Step 2: 2022: 60 > 50 → South is higher
Step 3: 2023: 65 < 70
Common mistake: (A), (C) and (D) are years in which North is higher.
Key point: Where two lines cross, their order changes.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A shop owner draws a chart of yearly sales (in ₹ lakh) of two branches:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
year = [2020, 2021, 2022, 2023]
north = [40, 55, 50, 70]
south = [30, 35, 60, 65]
plt.plot(year, north, color='green', linestyle='dashed', marker='o', label='North')
plt.plot(year, south, color='red', linewidth=3, label='South')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Sales')
plt.title('Branch Sales')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Question: What is the role of label='North' and label='South' in the code?
options: A) plt.legend() uses them to show which line belongs to which branch
B) They change the colour in which each of the two lines is drawn
C) They set the text that appears below the x-axis of the chart
D) They print each data value next to its point on the line
questions.explanation:
Answer: (A) plt.legend() uses them to show which line belongs to which branch
Why: The label argument gives each plotted line a name; plt.legend() then draws a box (the legend) that shows each line's style next to its name.
Why not the others: (B) Colour is set by color. (C) The x-axis title is set by plt.xlabel(). (D) Values are not written on the points by label.
Key point: Without label values, legend() has nothing to show.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A shop owner draws a chart of yearly sales (in ₹ lakh) of two branches:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
year = [2020, 2021, 2022, 2023]
north = [40, 55, 50, 70]
south = [30, 35, 60, 65]
plt.plot(year, north, color='green', linestyle='dashed', marker='o', label='North')
plt.plot(year, south, color='red', linewidth=3, label='South')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Sales')
plt.title('Branch Sales')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Question: How will the South line appear on the chart?
options: A) A green dashed line with circle markers
B) A thin red dashed line
C) A thick solid red line without markers
D) A red dotted line with circle markers
questions.explanation:
Answer: (C) A thick solid red line without markers
Given: The South call sets color='red' and linewidth=3 but no linestyle or marker.
Step 1: Colour → red
Step 2: linewidth=3 → thicker than the default
Step 3: The default linestyle is solid and no marker is drawn
Common mistake: (A) describes the North line. (B) and (D) borrow the North line's dashed style or markers.
Key point: Unspecified properties take their default values.

questions.question:
Read the following passage and answer the question that follows.

A shop owner draws a chart of yearly sales (in ₹ lakh) of two branches:

import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
year = [2020, 2021, 2022, 2023]
north = [40, 55, 50, 70]
south = [30, 35, 60, 65]
plt.plot(year, north, color='green', linestyle='dashed', marker='o', label='North')
plt.plot(year, south, color='red', linewidth=3, label='South')
plt.xlabel('Year')
plt.ylabel('Sales')
plt.title('Branch Sales')
plt.legend()
plt.show()

Question: Between which two consecutive years did North's sales increase the most?
questions.explanation:
Answer: (D) 2022 and 2023
Given: north = [40, 55, 50, 70].
Step 1: 2020 → 2021: 55 − 40 = +15
Step 2: 2021 → 2022: 50 − 55 = −5 (a fall)
Step 3: 2022 → 2023: 70 − 50 = +20 → largest increase
Common mistake: (A) is the second largest. (B) is a decrease. (C) are not consecutive years.
Key point: A steeper upward slope on a line plot means a larger increase.
